title: Innovation in Product Management
content:
Designing With Purpose: The Question Behind the Work

The habit that defines a good product person is not technical skill or creative flair — it is a persistent curiosity about why. Why are we building this? What is the point of it? Who benefits, and how? These questions can feel uncomfortable in organisations that reward output over reflection, but they are the foundation of work that actually matters. The alternative — copying another product, following a brief without questioning it, designing without understanding the business model — produces things that may be well-crafted but are ultimately purposeless.

An early lesson: working at one of the first online TV studios in London during the dot-com boom, a moment of genuine confusion about the company's right to exist. The screen was small. Connections were slow. Five hundred people were employed. An email to the CEO — one of those rare "ask me anything" moments — turned into a conversation about the business model and what it would take to make the product genuinely worth building. The point was not to challenge authority. It was that without understanding why a product exists, it is impossible to know whether the design decisions you are making are good ones.

The Innovation Curve and Why Products Disappear

Every product follows a curve. There is a period of growth, a peak, and — if the people building it stop innovating — a decline that can be slow or sudden depending on how fast the market moves. In some industries, the curve spans decades. In others, the fall can happen in a few years. But the direction is always the same for products that fail to evolve: down.

This is not a counsel of despair. It is an argument for continuous investment in innovation, even — especially — when things are going well. The companies and products that disappear are rarely the ones that failed dramatically. More often, they are the ones that succeeded for long enough to believe they did not need to change, and by the time the curve started falling, the gap between where they were and where they needed to be was too large to close. The product you are working on today will become obsolete. The question is whether you will have built something new before that happens.

Risk, Uncertainty, and the Personal Cost of Innovation

Trying out new ideas means taking risks. It means sticking your neck out, being wrong — often publicly — and doing it again anyway. Some people find this energising. Others find it genuinely threatening. Both responses are legitimate. What is not legitimate, from an organisational standpoint, is designing systems that punish the people who try.

The personal cost of innovation varies by personality and by context, but the organisational dimension is consistent: if trying something new and failing results in marginalisation or job loss, people will stop trying. They might do it once — curiosity or ambition overcoming caution — but they will remember what happened, and the second time they will think twice. The result is an organisation that talks about innovation while systematically discouraging it.

Building an Innovative Culture

Innovation at the organisational level is not primarily a question of hiring the right people, though that matters. It is a question of what gets rewarded. If experimentation is celebrated — if the person who ran a well-designed test on a hypothesis that turned out to be wrong is recognised for the rigour of their process rather than penalised for the outcome — then even people who are naturally risk-averse will start to participate. The culture follows from the incentives, not the other way around.

This means making it safe to be wrong, but not safe to be lazy. The distinction is important. A well-run experiment that generates a clear negative result is genuinely valuable. A vague initiative that never tested anything specific and therefore cannot produce learning is not. Building an innovative culture means creating the conditions for the former while being honest about the difference. When organisations get this right, innovation stops being the province of a few brave individuals and becomes something the whole organisation can do.
